Dividend yield is 0%, and two factors (revenue growth and price-to-book, 24% of the weight) could not be scored, so the result rests on incomplete data.

Net margin of 46.12% is still high, though down from 68.09% in 2024 and 59.34% in 2022

SAZEW.summary: Sazgar scores 86/100 mainly because sales and earnings have grown very fast over three years, margins are well above where they started, and the shares trade at a P/E of 3.8 against a sector median of about 7.8. The score rests on only 62% of the data: debt, liquidity, cash flow and working capital could not be scored. The share price is weak, trading below its 200-day average and lagging the KSE-100 by about 25 points over a year.
strengths: Sales rose from Rs 18.2bn to Rs 191.7bn over three years, and EPS from Rs 16.46 to Rs 390.51.
Net margin of 12.3% is far above the 5.5% at the start of the period, and the company has been profitable throughout.
Valuation looks cheap at P/E 3.8 versus a sector median of 7.85, and cash dividends were paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years.
risks: Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion cycle (about 38% of the score weight) are unscored, so the balance sheet and whether profits turn into cash are unknown.
Net margin fell from 15.0% to 12.3% in the latest year, and growth this steep may be hard to repeat or may reflect one-off conditions in the auto market.

The price is below its 200-day average and has lagged the market, and a P/E this low can mean the market doubts that earnings will last. The scorecard also flags that a bonus issue, split or one-off profit could distort the P/E and yield.

Check whether the latest profit includes one-off items, and whether any bonus issue or split affects the EPS, P/E and dividend yield comparisons.

GHNI.summary: Ghandhara Industries scores 86.1/100, driven by a sharp profit turnaround and a cheap valuation. Sales rose from about Rs 14.5 billion in 2023 to Rs 60.7 billion in 2026, and EPS went from Rs 4.21 to Rs 162.57. The P/E of 6.4 is below the sector median of 7.8. However, the scorecard has no debt, cash flow or liquidity data (62% coverage), so the score is only a partial picture.
strengths: Sales grew about 4x over three years and net margin widened from 1.23% to 11.42%.
P/E of 6.4 is below the sector median of 7.8, and the share price is above its 200-day average and well ahead of the KSE-100 over about a year.
Cash dividends were paid in both recorded years, and the payout rose from 100% to 120% of face value.
risks: Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion cycle (38% of the total weight) could not be scored, so balance sheet strain is invisible here.
Net margin slipped from 12.24% in 2025 to 11.42% in 2026, and a jump this large in a cyclical industry like auto assembly may not last; a low P/E may reflect profits the market expects to fall.
Dividend yield is only about 1.1%, so returns depend mostly on the share price. The growth history is also short, at four years of data.
checks: Check the balance sheet for borrowings, interest costs and current ratio, since rapid sales growth often needs heavy working capital.
Check the cash flow statement to confirm that the reported profits turned into actual operating cash, and look at inventory and receivables levels.
Read the September 2026 quarterly report and the corporate briefing presentation to see whether the high sales and margins are continuing and what drove the jump.

GAL.summary: Ghandhara Automobiles scores 77.4/100, driven mainly by very fast growth: sales rose from about Rs 10.0bn in 2023 to Rs 28.8bn in 2026, and net margin went from 0.63% to 12.02%. Valuation is roughly in line with its sector (P/E 7.9 vs 7.8) and the dividend is modest. About 38% of the scorecard, covering debt, liquidity, cash flow and working capital, could not be scored, so the score rests on a partial picture.
strengths: Sales grew about 42% a year over three years, and EPS moved from a loss of Rs 4.54 in 2024 to Rs 60.79 in 2026.
Net margin improved to 12.02% from 0.63% in 2023, showing much stronger profitability.
Valued at a P/E of 7.9, about the same as the sector median, and the price is above its 200-day average.
risks: Debt, liquidity, cash flow and cash conversion are all unscored, so leverage and whether profits turn into cash are unknown.
Earnings are volatile: 2024 was a loss-making year and the sales dip that year (Rs 5.4bn) shows how cyclical the business can be, so the recent surge may not persist.
The share trailed the KSE-100 by about 11 points over the past year, and the dividend yield is only 2.2%, so shareholders get a small cash return.
checks: Check the balance sheet in the 2026 annual report for borrowings, short-term debt and cash, since none of this was scored.
Check the cash flow statement to confirm that operating cash flow supports the reported Rs 3.5bn profit.
Read the quarter to September 2026 results (released Oct 27) to see whether the sales and margin gains are holding, and look at what drove the 2025-26 jump.

LOTCHEM.summary: The 48.2 score is held up by a cheap valuation (P/E 7.2 against a sector median of 9.9) and a very high dividend yield. Weak business trends pull it down: sales fell about 6.9% a year over three years, EPS dropped from Rs6.68 in 2022 to Rs0.74 in 2025, and net margin shrank from 10.09% to 1.38%. The price is also below its 200-day average and has lagged the KSE-100 by about 20 points over a year. Only 62% of the data is available, so the score leaves out debt, liquidity and cash flow.
strengths: Valuation looks low: P/E of 7.2 is about 0.73x the sector median of 9.9.
Recent cash dividends were announced (15% in July 2026 and 50% in January 2026), giving a stated yield of 24.6%.
The company is filing its quarterly results on time, with the September 2026 quarter filed in October.
risks: Profits have shrunk sharply: profit after tax fell from about Rs10.1bn in 2022 to Rs1.1bn in 2025, and sales fell from Rs109bn in 2024 to Rs81bn in 2025.
The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash flow or working capital, which together carry 38% of the weighting, so balance sheet strength is unknown.

The P/E of 7.2 and the 24.6% yield do not fit the latest annual EPS of Rs0.74 (about 33x at this price) or a payout that large. They may rest on newer quarterly profits, or on a one-off gain, which the scorecard flags as a possible distortion.
checks: Reconcile the P/E and dividend yield with the actual trailing EPS in the latest quarterly accounts, and check whether the payouts came from one-off profits or reserves.
Read the 2026 quarterly statements for the margin trend and for debt, cash flow and cash on hand, since the scorecard lacks them.
Read the September 2026 EGM resolutions and the 'Material Information' and 'Disclosure of Material Information' notices, which the data does not explain.

KOHC.summary: Kohat Cement scores 46.9 out of 100, which maps to a SELL signal, but only 62% of the data is available, so the score is incomplete. Sales have been flat (-0.3% a year over 3 years) and EPS has fallen about 26% a year, and the shares pay no dividend and have lagged the KSE-100 by 17.6 points over about a year. Against that, margins are much higher than three years ago and the P/E of 7.8 is slightly below the sector median of 8.4.

P/E of 7.8 is 0.93x the sector median of 8.4, a modest valuation discount
Price is above its 200-day average, which is a mildly positive trend signal

Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion are not scored because balance sheet and cash flow data are missing, so leverage and cash generation are unknown
No dividend yield and no recent payouts are shown, and the shares have underperformed the KSE-100 by 17.6 points over about a year

INIL.summary: INIL scores 43.6/100, which maps to a SELL signal. A 4.6% dividend yield is the one clearly positive factor. Only 62% of the scorecard could be calculated, so the score leaves out debt, liquidity and cash flow.
strengths: Dividend yield of 4.6%, with cash dividends paid in both fiscal years on record and a 50% payout announced in August 2026

Check the cash flow statement to see whether operating cash flow supports profits and the dividend

PSEL.summary: The score of 41.4/100 is held down mainly by price and payout. The P/E of 64.9 is about 3.7 times the sector median of 17.5, and no dividend is paid, so valuation (20% weight) and dividend (10% weight) both score zero. Sales growth is strong (about 29% a year over 3 years) and the company moved from loss to profit. But earnings have swung between loss and profit, and the net margin is thin at 2.83%. Debt, cash flow and liquidity are not scored, so about 38% of the weighting is unseen and the score rests on partial evidence (62% data coverage).
strengths: Sales more than doubled, from Rs 6.94bn in 2021 to Rs 15.04bn in 2024.
Returned to profit in 2024 (Rs 425m, EPS Rs 13.08) after a loss in 2023, and the net margin improved from -5.7% in 2021 to 2.83%.
Share price is above its 200-day average, though it has lagged the KSE-100 by about 17 points over a year.
risks: Earnings are unstable: losses in 2021 and 2023, profits in 2022 and 2024, so the 2024 profit may not be repeatable.
The valuation is demanding and no dividend is paid, so returns depend entirely on future growth in profit and price.
The scorecard cannot see debt, cash flow, working capital or liquidity. Fast sales growth with thin margins can hide heavy borrowing or cash strain.
checks: Check the latest annual and quarterly reports. The newest full-year figures here are for 2024, and the announcements mention extensions for holding the AGM for the year ended June 2025, so the FY2025 accounts may be late.
Reconcile the P/E: 64.9 does not match the 2024 EPS of Rs 13.08 at a price of Rs 1,366 (that would be about 104). Confirm which earnings figure the P/E uses.

Read the balance sheet and cash flow statement for borrowings, interest cover and operating cash flow. Also read the 'Material Information' and director-interest notices. Several announcement dates look inconsistent, so confirm them on the PSX site.

FFL.summary: Fauji Foods scores 38/100 mainly because the shares look expensive and have performed poorly, even though the business has improved a lot. Sales have grown about 33% a year and the company moved from a large loss in 2022 to a profit in 2025. However, the P/E of 36.8 is almost three times the sector median of 12.8, there is no dividend, and the price is below its 200-day average and well behind the KSE-100. Only 62% of the data was available, so debt, liquidity and cash flow are not reflected in the score.
strengths: Sales grew from Rs 12.4 billion in 2022 to Rs 28.9 billion in 2025, about 32.7% a year.
Turned from a Rs 2.17 billion loss in 2022 to a Rs 1.24 billion profit in 2025, with net margin up from -17.6% to 4.3%.
Profit and EPS have risen each year since 2022 (EPS Rs 0.26, 0.28, 0.49).
risks: Valuation is stretched: P/E of 36.8 versus a sector median of 12.8, so the price already assumes strong future growth.
Debt, liquidity, cash flow and working capital are not scored (about 38% of the weight), and the company has a history of losses, so financial strength is unknown.

Share price is below its 200-day average and trailed the KSE-100 by about 31.5 points over a year; no dividend is paid. Late-year announcements show an emergency board meeting and acting CEO and CFO appointments, which point to leadership change, though the reason is not given.

Find out why the emergency board meeting was called and why acting CEO and CFO were appointed, and whether permanent appointments are planned.

FFC.summary: FFC scores 84.2/100, driven by very strong sales and earnings growth over three years, a high dividend yield (9.2%) and a P/E of 10.2, slightly below the sector median of 10.9. The score rests on only 62% of the factors. Cash flow, debt, liquidity and cash conversion could not be scored, and together they carry 38% of the weight. The growth figures also look flattered by a big jump in 2024, and net margin has eased since 2023.
strengths: Sales rose from Rs 109.4bn (2022) to Rs 432.4bn (2025), and EPS from Rs 15.76 to Rs 51.69.
Dividend yield is 9.2%, with a cash dividend in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record and four cash payouts announced during 2026.
P/E of 10.2 is about 0.93x the sector median, a modest discount, and the price is above its 200-day average.
risks: Growth is slowing: sales rose about 134% in 2024 but only about 16% in 2025, and profit after tax rose about 14%. The 3-year average of 58% a year overstates the current pace.
Net margin slipped from 18.61% (2023) to 17.01% (2025), so profit is growing a little slower than sales.
The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash flow or cash conversion. A high dividend could be a strain if cash generation or borrowing is weak, and none of that is visible here.

Read the quarter-ended 30 Sep 2026 results (announced Oct 28, 2026) to see whether sales, margin and EPS are still growing or have flattened.
Compare total dividends declared against EPS, and check the face value, to judge how much of earnings is paid out and whether the yield can last.

FABL.summary: Faysal Bank scores 79.8/100, driven by strong growth (sales up 26.5% a year and EPS up 24.6% a year over three years), a 6.9% dividend yield paid in each of the last three years on record, and a P/E of 6.7 that is in line with the sector median. The score rests on only 62% of the possible data: price-to-book, asset quality and capital adequacy, which together carry 38% of the weight and matter most for a bank, are missing. The 'BUY' label is therefore provisional.
strengths: Fast three-year growth: sales up 26.5% a year and EPS up 24.6% a year, with net margin improving from 10.75% to 13.08%.
Dividend yield of 6.9%, with cash dividends in 3 of the last 3 fiscal years on record and several interim cash payouts announced in 2026.
Valuation is not stretched: P/E of 6.65 against a sector median of 6.74.
risks: The scorecard cannot see price-to-book, non-performing loan ratio or capital adequacy ratio, which are core measures of bank safety and value.

The most recent year shows slowing momentum: sales rose only about 1.4% in 2025, and profit after tax fell from Rs 23.0bn to Rs 21.7bn, with EPS dropping from 15.17 to 14.30. The 3-year growth figures flatter the current trend.

Price trend is neutral (score 50.3), only just above its 200-day average and +0.4 points versus the KSE-100, so the market is not showing strong confirmation. Debt, funding and cash flow data are also absent.

Check the capital adequacy ratio against the regulatory minimum, and whether it comfortably supports the current dividend payouts.
Read the Q3 2026 results to see why 2025 profit declined and whether earnings have recovered, and check book value to calculate price-to-book.

FHAM.summary: The 78.3 score is driven mainly by valuation: a P/E of 4.1 is about a quarter of the sector median of 16.2, and the 7.5% dividend yield also scores well. Growth looks good over three years (sales +11% a year, EPS +13% a year), but that hides a weaker recent picture: profit after tax fell from Rs 901m to Rs 748m in 2026 and EPS fell from 8.13 to 6.75. The share price is also weak, below its 200-day average and about 29 points behind the KSE-100 over a year, so the market appears to be doubting the cheap earnings.

JDWS.summary: The 77.7 score is driven mainly by a cheap valuation (P/E 5.2 against a sector median of 9.3) and fast sales growth of about 25% a year over three years. Cash dividends were paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record, with several interim payouts announced recently.

KTML.summary: KTML scores 44.2 out of 100, held back by a rich valuation (P/E 11.0 against a sector median of 7.2), a weak price trend (below its 200-day average and about 43 points behind the KSE-100 over a year), and EPS that has fallen over three years. Cash dividends paid in both years on record, with the latest at 100% of face value, though the yield is only 1.7%.

The share price has done about 14 points better than the KSE-100 over roughly a year, even though it sits below its 200-day average.
